college.stem: In an experiment by German and Defeyter (2000), children had to turn a box over and use it as a support to help a toy bear reach a toy on a high shelf. Some children had first seen the box used as a container. How did the 5-year-olds perform in that condition?
options: They were not slowed by the earlier container use and were faster than the older children.
They were slowed more than the older children by the earlier container use.
They were slowed just as much as the older children by the earlier container use.
They failed to solve the task after seeing the container use, unlike older children.
college.why: German and Defeyter (2000) found 5-year-olds immune to the container demonstration; 6- and 7-year-olds were slower.

simple.stem: German and Defeyter (2000) showed some children a box being used as a container before asking them to use it as a support. Which children were NOT slowed by this?
options: Five-year-olds were not slowed by the container use.
Seven-year-olds were not slowed by the container use.
Six-year-olds were not slowed by the container use.
Every age group was slowed by the container use.
simple.why: The 5-year-olds were immune; 6- and 7-year-olds were slower after the container use.

college.stem: A person cannot see that a box could be used as a platform because they think of it only as a container. What is this called?
options: Functional fixedness, being stuck on an object's usual function and missing another possible use.
Perseveration, repeating an earlier response after the situation has changed.
Insight, suddenly seeing the whole solution after being stuck.
Attribute substitution, answering an easier question in place of a harder one.
college.why: This is functional fixedness. The other terms are different concepts.

options: Being stuck on an object's usual function and failing to see new uses.
Being unable to remember where an object was last placed.
Choosing the first option offered in a decision.
Solving a problem by suddenly seeing the answer.
simple.why: Functional fixedness means being stuck on an object's usual function.

college.stem: Why did German and Defeyter (2000) test some children after showing the box used as a container and others without that experience?
options: To see whether showing the usual container use slowed children from seeing the box as a support.
To see whether children liked the toy bear more after seeing the container use.
To see whether children could remember the box from one day to the next.
To see whether children preferred containers to supports when given a choice.
college.why: The container demonstration tests whether the usual function interferes; the no-demonstration condition shows baseline improvement with age.

simple.stem: What was the container demonstration in the box task meant to test?
options: Whether seeing the box's usual use makes it harder to use it as a support.
Whether children can lift heavy boxes without help.
Whether children remember a toy bear's name.
Whether children enjoy playing with boxes.
simple.why: It tests functional fixedness: whether the usual function interferes with a new use.

college.stem: Leist and colleagues (2022) played speech to be ignored while children and adults remembered either words in order or locations in order. Which result did they obtain?
options: Speech hurt memory for the verbal order task but spatial order memory was not disrupted.
Speech hurt memory for the verbal and spatial tasks about equally.
Speech hurt spatial order memory but left verbal order memory unaffected.
Speech hurt only the adults, in both the verbal and the spatial tasks.
college.why: The speech effect was specific to verbal material in Leist and colleagues (2022).

simple.stem: What did Leist and colleagues (2022) find when ignored speech was played during verbal and spatial memory tasks?
options: It hurt verbal memory but not spatial memory.
It hurt spatial memory but not verbal memory.
It hurt both kinds of memory equally.
It hurt neither kind of memory.
simple.why: Speech impaired verbal but not spatial recall.

college.stem: Which speech disrupts serial recall most in the irrelevant speech effect?
options: Changing-state speech, made of different syllables, disrupts recall more than repeated-syllable speech.
Steady-state speech, made of one repeated syllable, disrupts recall more than changing speech.
Speech played in a language the listener understands, but only if it is loud.
Speech that the listener attends to closely, regardless of its syllables.
college.why: Changing-state speech (different syllables) disrupts recall more than steady-state speech.

options: Speech made of different syllables that change from one to the next.
Speech made of one syllable repeated over and over.
Speech that gets louder over time.
Speech that the listener is asked to remember.
simple.why: Changing-state speech has different syllables; steady-state speech repeats one syllable.

college.stem: What did the spatial memory task let Leist and colleagues (2022) tell apart?
options: Whether speech disrupts memory for order of any kind or only for verbal material.
Whether children or adults have better hearing for ignored speech.
Whether steady-state speech is louder than changing-state speech.
Whether verbal memory is stored in a different country than spatial memory.
college.why: The spatial task separates accounts predicting disruption for any item from one limited to verbal material.

simple.stem: Why include a spatial memory task in a study of ignored speech?
options: To check whether speech disrupts only verbal memory or all kinds of memory.
To make the task easier for the children taking part.
To test whether the participants can hear the speech.
To keep the experiment shorter.
simple.why: Spatial items show whether the speech effect is specific to verbal material.

options: Using actions such as writing things down to reduce the mental demands of a task.
Repeating a list silently so that it stays active in the mind.
Forgetting information on purpose because it is no longer needed.
Grouping items into larger meaningful chunks to remember more.
college.why: Cognitive offloading means using external actions to reduce mental demands.

options: Using actions like writing things down to reduce mental effort.
Repeating items silently to remember them.
Forgetting things on purpose.
Grouping items into chunks.
simple.why: Offloading uses external actions to reduce mental demands.

college.stem: In the work of Morrison and Richmond (2020), how did the length of a letter list relate to offloading?
options: Longer lists made people offload more, and offloading helped most for the longer lists.
Longer lists made people offload less, and offloading helped most for the shorter lists.
List length did not change how much people offloaded or how much it helped.
Longer lists made offloading harmful, so memory-only recall was better.
college.why: Offloading increased with load and benefited memory most at high loads.

simple.stem: What did Morrison and Richmond (2020) find about offloading when lists got longer?
options: People offloaded more and it helped more.
People offloaded less and it helped less.
People offloaded the same amount at every length.
People offloaded more but it made memory worse.
simple.why: Offloading and its benefit both grew with load.

college.stem: Which pattern did Morrison and Richmond (2020) report about memory ability and offloading?
options: Memory ability did not predict who offloaded.
Weaker memory ability strongly predicted who offloaded.
Stronger memory ability predicted who offloaded.
Memory ability predicted offloading only in the longest lists.
college.why: No link between memory ability and who offloaded was found.

simple.stem: Did memory ability predict who offloaded in the work of Morrison and Richmond (2020)?
options: No, memory ability did not predict who offloaded.
Yes, weaker memory predicted more offloading.
Yes, stronger memory predicted more offloading.
Yes, but only for the shortest lists.
simple.why: Memory ability did not predict offloading.

college.stem: What is one explanation for the intuitive error on the bat-and-ball problem?
options: Reasoners unconsciously swap in an easier problem and neglect the words 'more than'.
Reasoners deliberately choose the wrong answer to save time.
Reasoners cannot do the arithmetic needed to find the right answer.
Reasoners misremember the total cost of the bat and ball.
college.why: One account is unconscious attribute substitution.

options: Swapping in an easier question for the harder one that was asked.
Replacing a missing object with a similar one.
Choosing the option that was preselected.
Repeating a response that worked before.
simple.why: Attribute substitution means answering an easier problem without noticing.

college.stem: What did Hoover and Healy (2019) conclude about how people make the bat-and-ball error?
options: The error is conscious: people notice and remember the words 'more than' but do not use their meaning.
The error is unconscious: people never notice the words 'more than' at all.
The error is arithmetic: people cannot subtract and divide correctly.
The error is due to confidence: people simply guess without looking at the problem.
college.why: Incorrect reasoners recalled and recognized the phrase but did not integrate its meaning.

simple.stem: What did Hoover and Healy (2019) find about the wrong answer to the bat-and-ball problem?
options: People remembered the words 'more than' but did not use their meaning.
People never noticed the words 'more than'.
People could not do the arithmetic.
People guessed without looking at the problem.
simple.why: The phrase was recalled but its meaning was not integrated.

college.stem: Why use a control problem without the words 'more than'?
options: To check whether reasoners who answered wrongly were less confident when the phrase was present.
To check whether reasoners can do arithmetic when there are no words.
To check whether reasoners read faster when problems are shorter.
To check whether the cost of the bat and ball affects confidence.
college.why: The control lacks the phrase, so any confidence drop on the standard problem can be tied to it.

simple.stem: What did the control problem without 'more than' show about incorrect reasoners?
options: They were less confident on the standard problem than on the control.
They were more confident on the standard problem than on the control.
They were equally confident on both problems.
They solved the control problem correctly every time.
simple.why: Lower confidence on the standard problem showed they sensed something was wrong.

college.stem: In the work of Giuliani and colleagues (2023), which default changed choices?
options: Making the risky option the default increased risk taking.
Making the sure option the default increased risk aversion.
Making either option the default changed choices equally.
Neither default changed choices at all.
college.why: A risky default raised risk taking; a sure default did not raise risk aversion.

simple.stem: What did Giuliani and colleagues (2023) find when the risky option was the default?
options: People took more risks.
People took fewer risks.
People took the same risks as with no default.
People refused to choose anything.
simple.why: A risky default raised risk taking.

college.stem: Giuliani and colleagues (2023) asked people afterward where they thought a default came from. Which belief went with rejecting the default most often?
options: Seeing the default as what previous respondents chose or as the result of chance.
Seeing the default as the most rational choice.
Seeing the default as the safest and surest option.
Seeing the default as a mistake in the survey.
college.why: Those who thought the default came from previous respondents or chance tended to reject it most often.

simple.stem: Which belief about a default went with people rejecting it most often?
options: That it came from previous respondents or from chance.
That it was the most rational choice.
That it was the safest option.
That it was a mistake in the survey.
simple.why: Seeing the default as coming from previous respondents or chance went with rejecting it most often.

college.stem: What did Chein and colleagues (2011) conclude about how peers raise risk taking in adolescents?
options: The peer effect went with more activity in the brain's reward circuitry, while cognitive-control regions did not change.
The peer effect went with less activity in cognitive-control regions, while reward circuitry did not change.
Peers directly pressure adolescents, which shows up in motor regions of the brain.
Peers have no effect on the brain, so the extra risk comes from boredom.
college.why: Reward regions responded to peers; cognitive-control regions did not change with peer presence.

simple.stem: What did Chein and colleagues (2011) find happens in the adolescent brain when friends watch?
options: Reward-related brain regions become more active.
Cognitive-control brain regions become less active.
Visual brain regions become more active.
Nothing changes in the brain.

college.stem: What did the 'alone' condition give Chein and colleagues (2011) to compare with the 'friends watching' condition?
options: A baseline showing how much peer presence changes risk taking and brain activity.
A baseline showing how skilled each person is at real-world driving.
A baseline showing how much each person likes the friends who watch.
A baseline showing how fast the brain scanner collects data.
college.why: Alone versus watched shows the specific change caused by peers.

simple.stem: Why compare playing alone with playing while friends watched?
options: To see what changes in risk taking when peers are present.
To see which friends are better drivers.
To see how tired people get.
To see which game is harder.
simple.why: The comparison isolates the effect of peer presence.
